stp.prompt: One network, three attack waves, one budget for the whole night. Every control in the shop lists what it can actually do — attacks resolve against those properties, not against the control's name.
stp.hint: The full-coverage build exists and costs exactly par. Cheap now can be expensive later: the wave-2 traffic remembers what the wave-1 bargain could not see.

stp-c-anomips.label: Anomaly-based NIPS
stp-c-anomips.definition: Inline prevention that learns a baseline of normal traffic and blocks significant deviations — no signature required, more tuning required.
stp-c-anomips.why: Anomaly detection is the counter to novel attacks: it flags behavior that departs from the baseline instead of looking up a pattern, which is exactly what a zero-day never has.

stp-c-harden.label: Hardened server baseline
stp-c-harden.definition: The unglamorous control: unnecessary services removed, default credentials gone, patches current, configuration locked to a documented baseline.
stp-c-harden.why: Hardening shrinks the attack surface itself, so an exploit aimed at a service that is disabled, patched, or locked down has nothing to land on — protection that does not depend on recognizing the attack.

stp-c-mailgw.label: Mail security gateway
stp-c-mailgw.definition: Scrubs inbound mail before the relay accepts it: attachment detonation, link rewriting, spoofing checks, and sender authentication.
stp-c-mailgw.why: Mail rides its own protocol path into the DMZ, so web- and port-focused controls never inspect it; a dedicated gateway on the mail seat is what stands between a lure and an inbox.

stp-c-ngfw.label: Next-generation firewall
stp-c-ngfw.definition: Deep-packet appliance: everything the stateful firewall does, plus application awareness and outbound traffic control in a single (expensive) box.
stp-c-ngfw.why: An NGFW identifies the application inside the flow rather than trusting the port number, and can police egress — breadth in one seat, at a price that forces a budget decision.

stp-c-pktfilter.label: Packet-filter firewall
stp-c-pktfilter.definition: First-generation rule list: permits or drops each packet by source, destination, and port, one packet at a time, with no memory of any conversation.
stp-c-pktfilter.why: A static packet filter is the cheapest gate at a choke point, but because it inspects packets in isolation it cannot tell a legitimate reply from an unsolicited flood — state-based attacks walk past it.

stp-c-proxy.label: Forward proxy
stp-c-proxy.definition: Terminates outbound connections on behalf of internal hosts: nothing inside talks to the internet directly, and the proxy logs, filters, and can refuse every request.
stp-c-proxy.why: Mediating egress is the control that catches traffic leaving — beaconing malware included. Inbound-facing defenses never see an outbound channel; a proxy exists on exactly that path.

stp-c-signips.label: Signature NIPS
stp-c-signips.definition: Inline network intrusion prevention matching traffic against a database of known attack patterns. Blocks what it recognizes — and only what it recognizes.
stp-c-signips.why: Signature detection is precise and cheap against published attacks, and an inline placement can block rather than merely alert. Its blind spot is definitional: an attack with no signature yet does not match anything.

stp-c-stateful.label: Stateful inspection firewall
stp-c-stateful.definition: Third-generation firewall: tracks every conversation in a state table, so a packet is judged by the connection it belongs to, not just its header fields.
stp-c-stateful.why: Keeping a state table is what lets a firewall drop half-open floods and unsolicited traffic that a stateless rule list would wave through — the classic upgrade at the perimeter choke point.

stp-c-switchsec.label: Switch security bundle
stp-c-switchsec.definition: VLAN segmentation plus 802.1X port authentication on the switch fabric: traffic is fenced into segments, and a device must authenticate before its wall port carries anything.
stp-c-switchsec.why: Segmentation decides how far one compromised host can reach, and port-based network access control decides whether an unknown device gets a link at all — both live in the switch, not at the perimeter.

stp-c-waf.label: Web application firewall
stp-c-waf.definition: Sits in front of a web server and reads the HTTP payload itself — queries, parameters, headers — blocking requests whose content attacks the application.
stp-c-waf.why: Port 443 is legitimately open, so packet, stateful, and even application-identifying firewalls pass a well-formed HTTPS request; only payload inspection sees the injection inside it. That is the WAF's whole job.

stp-fb-sqli.why: Application-layer attacks arrive inside allowed traffic; only payload inspection on the web seat answers them.

stp-fb-sweep.why: A deny-by-default filter at the choke point makes closed ports invisible to scanning.

stp-w1-phish.why: Mail enters on its own protocol path, so firewalls tuned for web traffic never read it; a mail security gateway on that path is the control that stops the lure before a human can click it.

stp-w1-sqli.why: An application-layer attack arrives inside allowed traffic; only a control that inspects the HTTP payload itself — a WAF — can tell a malicious request from a legitimate one on the same port.

stp-w1-sweep.why: A firewall at the perimeter choke point is the control that answers scanning: any deny-by-default filter makes closed ports invisible instead of chatty.

stp-w2-lateral.why: Segmentation is the control that decides blast radius — perimeter devices never see east-west traffic, so the fence has to live in the switch fabric itself.

stp-w2-synflood.why: A SYN flood is invisible to per-packet rules because every packet is individually well-formed; only connection-state tracking notices that the handshakes never finish.

stp-w2-worm.why: A published, fingerprinted attack is signature detection's home game: cheap, precise, and low-noise — the economical pick when the threat is known.

stp-w3-beacon.why: Inbound-facing controls never inspect the outbound path; egress mediation is the distinct control that catches command-and-control traffic leaving the network.

stp-w3-rogue.why: Port-based network access control (802.1X) authenticates the device before the port passes traffic; without it, physical access to a socket is network access.

stp-w3-zeroday.why: A zero-day defeats signature databases by definition; what answers it is reducing the surface it needs (hardening) or flagging the deviation it causes (anomaly detection) — recognition of the attack is never available.
